words.text: Today you build the idea words yourself, and watch what happens to each base word. Match the fort and val words to their meanings. Then write a paragraph with five transitions. Six more pans.

reading.text: Read Chapter 12, Bullwhip. Walk home with the partners by the campfires. Then watch what Praiseworthy does when the truth and his welcome pull different ways.

assignment.text: Three questions, the last one about all three chapters. Then revise your literary response with the checklist. Make sure each piece of evidence is a character's choice.

game.title: Pan for Color
game.sub: This week's word game · 6 pans today
game.look: Each pan holds four words from the diggings. Two are color, the real gold. Two are slickens, the mud. Tap the slickens to wash them over the side. When only gold is left, the spangles slide into Jack's pouch.

do: Read the clue on the pan.
Tap a word that does not belong to wash it out.
Keep going until only gold is left.
Tap Next pan.

virtue.name: honesty
virtue.title: The honesty meter
virtue.intro: Think about one moment from Chapter 12.
virtue.moment: The miners say Praiseworthy knocked the outlaw nineteen feet uphill. First he tries to explain that Mr. Fletcher spread a grossly exaggerated account. When no one will listen, he winks at Jack and says it looked twenty-three feet at least.
virtue.ask: How honest is Praiseworthy here? Slide to show.
virtue.take: Mason's take: somewhere in the middle. He tries to tell the truth first, and he never lies about the punch itself. But then he plays along with a tall tale, and he winks while he does it. Fleischman makes it funny, and leaves you to decide where honesty ends and a good joke begins.

art.title: Sunday Morning in the Mines (detail)
art.alt: A painting of three miners resting outside a log cabin under pine trees; one reads aloud from a book, inside the doorway a man writes a letter, and a small cooking fire and a wooden rocker sit on the ground in front.
art.look: Charles Nahl was a miner and artist in the gold country. He painted this in 1872. This is one part of a larger painting: on their day off, these miners read, rest and write letters home by the cabin. Look at the fire, the pans and the wooden rocker on the ground. It is the kind of camp the partners walk back to in Chapter 12.
